Meanwhile, the company recently launched Nerve, a job marketplace where gamers earn money using their own rigs — an attempt to give a stake to the generation most exposed to AI displacement.

Laura Miele, head of corporate development at Electronic Arts, believes that as artificial intelligence grows in game development, it strips out tedious grunt work and speeds up the whole process, leading to "a real rise in creativity."
Miele shared this view earlier this month at the Game Business Live showcase during Summer Game Fest, when asked whether more AI tools would shorten development cycles across the board.

"Perhaps in some parts they will," Miele said. "I really believe in what I've seen, that I'm pretty excited about. I've always wanted to help our studio developers remove friction and I've always kind of wanted to be a hero to them and help them create career-defining experiences."

"And I think that AI, what I've seen, how AI has enabled removing friction from our pipelines and our tools and our workflows, has been pretty exciting. It's removed some tedium out of their jobs. And I've seen faster prototyping. I've seen faster creativity and shorter, faster conversations around creativity and coming to alignment. So, we're seeing it and I think there's a real rise of creativity that comes from removing some of the tedious tasks out of development."

It's not entirely clear what kind of AI is being referenced here. There's a wide gap between an AI-based project management tool like the one used by Shadow of the Colossus director Fumito Ueda at Genki Design, and the generative AI slop machines that have crept into nearly every corner.

Still, EA has never hidden its enthusiasm for generative AI. CEO Andrew Wilson, for instance, said in 2024 that the company was "embracing [generative AI] deeply" and that "about 60% of all of our development processes have high feasibility to be positively impacted by generative AI."

EA is also reportedly counting on AI to help lower operating costs, as it works to service $20 billion in debt financing taken on during Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund's $55 billion acquisition of the company. (If you're wondering why EA, the company being acquired, is taking on billions in debt to help pay for its own acquisition, PC Gamer's finance expert Lincoln Carpenter has broken it down. Short version: everyone's scared.)

Employees reportedly aren't as enthusiastic about this AI-centric future. Some suspect the company is using AI to justify layoffs. AI-related or not, EA has cut hundreds of jobs at BioWare and Respawn, and shut down Cliffhanger Games entirely, since the Saudi investment was announced in September 2025. The most recent round of layoffs reportedly happened earlier this week, with the number of people affected not disclosed.

Industry experts and Unreal Engine developers are divided over Epic Games' State of Unreal reveal. Unreal Engine 5.8, early UE6 details, MCP-based AI workflows, Verse, and the eventual move away from Blueprints were all put under scrutiny.

The strongest impression many developers took away is that Epic isn't treating UE 5.8 and UE6 as just another renderer, workflow, or performance update. The company is laying the groundwork for a broader production shift centered on AI-assisted workflows, Verse, interoperable content, and a tighter relationship between Unreal Engine and UEFN. In other words, Epic appears to be taking a big step toward the metaverse engine it has long envisioned.

In its official roadmap, Epic said UE6 will improve rendering, cut cook times, tighten the iteration loop, and boost mobile performance. At the same time, it aims to change how games are shipped and operated through Verse, open standards, interoperable content, and MCP integration for tools like Claude and Gemini.

First, the features coming in UE 5.8 excited developers. Mesh terrain was impressive, Lumen Lite aimed at lower-end devices like the Switch 2 was welcomed as a sign of optimization, and Lore, a new open-source version control system, also drew interest. Bjornar Hoff of Rainiere Virtual called it "My favourite bit of the show!" and noted that UE6 merges UEFN and UE into the same product line.

Brian J. Pohl, a former Epic employee now lead visualization artist at [namethemachine], called this AI-integration-focused news a key "turning point" for the industry. Matthew J.X. Doyle of Falswork said the keynote's "real throughline" was UE5 and UEFN converging into a "foundation-first" engine built on Verse and distributed software transactional memory.

The most contentious point is that Actors and Blueprints will eventually be phased out, replaced by a new Verse-based structure using Scene Graph. Anton Mikhailenko of Keyboard Katz Studio argued that a non-visual scripting language is easier to maintain, optimize, and merge, making it better suited for large teams. He noted that Epic is betting on widespread LLM use throughout UE6's lifespan.

Optimism wasn't universal. Some developers and artists read the same announcement as a sign of a far more disruptive shift than Epic's framing suggested. The clearest practical worry is Blueprints' future. In the roadmap, Epic said it will keep Actors and Blueprints in early UE6 versions but phase them out "eventually" once the new framework matures, with conversion tools to help migrate projects.

Epic is targeting late 2027 for UE6 early access, with full release expected 12 to 18 months later. That means no immediate break, but the long-term direction is clear. Since Blueprints has symbolized Unreal's accessibility for years, questions arose immediately. Indeed, Game of the Year winner "Clair Obscur: Expedition 33" was possible because a small team built its entire gameplay system in Blueprints.

Steve Vegan, senior technical artist at Industrial Light & Magic, was sharper still. "The joy in creation does not come from the volume of output. It comes from the art process. Tools like this exist to remove the creation process entirely." Chris Geislerjohnson, a former Epic, Infinity Ward, and Rebellion UI artist, also called moving away from Blueprints, which has lowered the barrier to entry, "risky."

Epic sought to ease those concerns, saying its philosophy is to bring existing projects along and that it won't "force a hard break." Still, the fact remains that Scene Graph, UE6's new gameplay framework, is being built fresh on top of Verse from the ground up. As Tim Sweeney put it, "UE5 plus UEFN equals UE6," so time will tell how projects currently in development weather the change.

The goal goes beyond rendering or performance gains. It's about building once and shipping to PC, console, mobile, Fortnite, and even other UE6-based ecosystems. For small teams and live-service developers, that could mean faster iteration, wider distribution, and content that's easier to move around. But AI-assisted editor control, Verse-based systems, interoperable content, and distribution through Fortnite also raise real questions about training, maintenance, copyright, team roles, and production policy.

Poncle, maker of "Vampire Survivors," said it is taking another look at its planned Fortnite collaboration. The statement came right after Epic Games announced it would add AI features to Unreal Engine.

The studio wrote this on Reddit: "Following today's news about gen-AI usage by Epic to create all sort of game assets, including Fortnite characters, we're currently 'reviewing' our collaboration with Fortnite."

Epic had just unveiled four new Fortnite crossovers, one of which was Vampire Survivors content. But the studio's concern is what Epic announced in the same breath: integrating generative AI into Unreal Engine 6, which includes tools like Claude and Gemini.

According to Epic executive Marcus Wassmer, these AI features are designed as "creativity and productivity multipliers" that help development teams focus on core creative work. Epic demonstrated artists using generative AI to concept Fortnite characters and environments.

This episode reflects the industry's hesitation about adopting AI. Earlier surveys found about half of game developers view generative AI negatively, worried it could harm game quality and the industry as a whole.

This morning, Chengdu-based independent studio Jotoyo Games unveiled its debut title, Monster Fantasy. Jotoyo is a team of about 20 people, but combined they carry "decades" of industry experience. The studio is preparing for a PC launch following a Kickstarter campaign starting July 15. Its Steam page is already live.

blocks.cap: Monster Fantasy key visual

blocks.x: Drawing inspiration from hits like Monster Hunter, Stardew Valley, Animal Crossing and Pokémon, it weaves free-form monster hunting together with town-building and life simulation in a colorful chibi art style.

Players become an amnesiac hero in the Kingdom of Eldoras, a vast fantasy world spanning valleys, rainforests, frozen plains and volcanoes. The kingdom serves as a setting where monster-hunting adventure unfolds alongside quiet village life. Monster Fantasy's core design splits the game into two fully separate modules, combat and life simulation, each with its own progression path.

No one is forced into either path. Hardcore hunters and purely laid-back farmers alike can finish the campaign. In the words of founder Allan Xai, the studio's goal is to "break down the barrier between action games and cozy games," creating a space that brings core and casual players together.

In combat, players choose from four classes, each with its own feel. The Warrior wields heavy gear, moving between offense and defense with precise guarding. The Mage combines elements to craft and cast their own spells. The Archer focuses on literal long-range precision combat, while the Swordsman is another melee character built around evasion-based, agile action. Skills are tied to individual weapons, though, so a single character can eventually unlock the skills of every class. You can specialize in one path or master all four.

Combat has plenty of variables too. Day-night cycles and weather affect monster behavior, rewarding players who study the ecology before engaging. Villagers can be recruited as combat companions, though not all of them are suited for fighting. Over 50 species of giant monsters populate Eldoras, each with distinct habits and exploitable weaknesses.
Defeated monsters can also be tamed and kept as pets. They grow from juvenile forms, gain new abilities over time, and some become mounts used for travel and cooperative combat.

Players name and run their own village, build houses, and decorate their settlement to their taste. Monster Fantasy features about 100 unique villagers you can befriend, each with different personalities, strengths and interests. You can bring the ones you like into your village and recruit them for work or combat. On top of that, an AI-driven conversation system powered by LLM and TTS technology lets you hold recruitment talks, bargaining and everyday chat in real-time free form.
A release date has not yet been set.
Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney said Valve's AI labeling requirement for developers on Steam is "really irresponsible" and fuels a "hater community."

Earlier this month, Sweeney and Epic staff took the stage at Unreal Fest to reveal the first details of Unreal Engine 6. One core message was that Epic isn't avoiding generative AI use, but rather intends to support its use in the game development process.

blocks.cap: Tim Sweeney at GDC

blocks.x: As his social media posts already showed, this remark extends a pattern of Sweeney supporting and defending AI in games. Going further this time, Sweeney took direct aim at how Valve handles AI and how it requires disclosure of AI use on Steam.

As ResetEra user Alexandros noted, PC Gamer interviewed Sweeney right after the State of Unreal presentation. During the interview, he talked about how expensive and difficult it is for developers to create assets, pointing to AI as an economical way to get assets with a "unique look and feel."

Sweeney went on to say that developers are in a position where they must submit to Steam to promote their games, and that it's "unfortunate" that a game gets a "Scarlet Letter of AI" if AI was used during development. The result, he said, is a "hater community trying to kill the game."

Sweeney views Valve's AI-labeling warning as "really irresponsible," saying it lowers developers' chances of success and that Valve "shouldn't do it." In short, he believes developers shouldn't be made to disclose AI use in game development the way they are now, arguing it sets developers up to fail from the start.

Sweeney is right that games that disclose AI use face fierce backlash — look at Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis. Still, given environmental costs and the absence of human creation, it's not strange for gamers to keep their distance. Unfortunately, AI shows little sign of slowing down, but most would agree that it's still better for Valve to disclose the facts than not.

Sjoerd De Jong, an expert who worked with Unreal Engine from its earliest days, has left Epic Games. He joined as a full-time employee in 2014, starting out as "lead evangelist," and most recently served as senior director on an unannounced project. He announced his departure in a LinkedIn post last week.

"After 27 years of Unreal Engine, and 12 years at Epic Games and Unreal Engine I have decided to move on. Last week was my last week at Epic," De Jong wrote. "This has been an awesome ride that has been truly life changing in so many ways. I didn't have an easy childhood or youth and things weren't going anywhere, but all of that changed entirely when I discovered Unreal Engine."

blocks.cap: State of Unreal Chicago 2026, where Unreal Engine 6 was revealed

blocks.x: His connection to Unreal goes back to when he was 15, modding the original 1998 FPS. As a standout mapmaker, he joined the work on Unreal Tournament 2004 through a direct offer from Epic, designing levels like DM-Rankin and ONS-Torlan. According to server statistics compiled on the Unreal wiki, DM-Rankin is the most-played UT2004 map of all time. His personal site's portfolio also features other work like Killzone and The Ball at a glance.

He passed through several studios, including Starbreeze and his own indie company Teotl Studios, but Unreal Engine remained his long-running passion and specialty. That's why Epic brought him on in 2014, calling him the engine's "lead evangelist."

In the LinkedIn post, he described how much life changed while working with multiple generations of the engine at Epic. "Dozens of countries visited, hundreds of studios visited, hundreds of talks presented, tens of thousands of people met, and millions of developers supported every year."

As for why he's decided to leave now, he wrote that "this era has come to a close, and it is time to move forward." "The games industry has always been an industry where change is relentless and inevitable, but it feels like we are reaching a pivotal point now and a potent mix of things."

Epic recently unveiled its plans for Unreal Engine 6, which merges Unreal Engine 5 and Unreal Editor for Fortnite, with heavy emphasis on open standards that let content, code and economies port and interoperate across games, ecosystems and engines, as well as generative AI integration. Looking ahead, De Jong said that for him, the strategic path is to accept the direction the industry is heading, work through the challenges and opportunities it presents, and find a way to adapt and do well.

At State of Unreal 2026, livestreamed from Unreal Fest in Chicago, Epic Games announced the release of Unreal Engine 5.8 while going in depth on Unreal Engine 6, which it had first teased briefly last month at the Rocket League Championship Series 2026 in Paris.

blocks.cap: Unreal Engine 6 × Unreal Editor for Fortnite

blocks.x: Founder, CEO and majority shareholder Tim Sweeney took the stage to explain that UE6 is not just about improved rendering or world-building, but about changing how games are launched and operated altogether. The idea is that once something is built with Unreal Engine 6, it becomes a game that can be released on any console, PC or mobile store, and can also connect live with the Fortnite ecosystem or with games other developers have made with UE6.

So UE6 merges UE5 and Unreal Editor for Fortnite into a single engine, but that's just the tip of the iceberg. The new engine is underpinned by Verse, a new programming language designed for massive persistent worlds, where the runtime handles global state and transactional concurrency. Scene Graph is UE6's gameplay framework, built from the ground up on top of Verse, aimed at interoperable components that different games can reuse.

The part likely to draw the most attention is the integration of LLMs into Unreal Engine 6. Using an MCP (Model Context Protocol) plugin, Epic exposes a wide range of the engine's functionality to whichever model you want, whether that's Claude, Gemini or a custom model.

blocks.cap: A rendering of an Unreal city, with code and editor menus visible in the lower right of the screen

blocks.x: This is an optional workflow layer inside Unreal, where the model helps with content creation while developers keep control. The model doesn't replace the editor; it works through the editor, and everything can still be edited directly in Unreal. When a developer feeds it a prompt or task, the model examines and makes changes to the scene via MCP. In the demo, Epic showed furnishing a room, scaling that up to city size, laying down roads and buildings, then refining lighting, materials and effects.

In its UE6 blog post, Epic wrote, "Thus, for UE6, we see LLMs, generative AI models, and tools like Claude and Codex playing a central role in helping you build content faster while maintaining the creative control you need." The idea is not to keep AI as a separate tool on the side, but to weave it into content creation itself. For game teams, that means models assisting with level assembly, character setup, code help, crash analysis and test generation.

LLMs are weak at handling spatial reasoning, but Epic filled that gap by providing more than 80 procedural content generation primitives, an example library, and Skills covering specific Unreal workflows. Above all, everything stays under developer control, so it's up to the developer how much help they take from the LLM. The MCP server, the PCG Primitive Plugin, and custom-built Skills were in fact already shipped today as part of 5.8. UE6's early access target is late 2027, with full release 12 to 18 months after that, putting it at late 2028 at the earliest and, realistically, 2029.

blocks.cap: Command & Conquer: Generals – Zero Hour running on an iPad (Image: Ammaar Reshi)

blocks.x: It was only a few days ago that Anthropic released Claude Fable 5 after a temporary access restriction in the US. That model has already been used to port the 2003 game Command & Conquer: Generals – Zero Hour to iOS. The port reportedly needed the source code, earlier ports, and human tweaking to work.

The news came from Ammaar Reshi, a product and design lead at Google AI Studio, who posted it on X on July 4. Reshi said the port stands on earlier ports and modernization work, describing it as having "had a chain of giants to stand on." He forked directly from a Linux/Mac build made by The Super Hackers.

Reshi's announcement read: "I used Fable 5 to port Command & Conquer: Generals Zero Hour to the iPhone and iPad! This is the actual 2003 engine compiled for ARM64 natively, no emulator. Campaign, skirmish, Generals Challenge all work with touch controls built for an RTS."

What makes this port unusual is the simple fact that it runs on iOS at all. New touch controls built for an RTS were added as well, letting players tap to select, drag to draw a selection box, and long-press to deselect. Anyone who wants to try it can get it from GitHub, though they'll need to supply their own copy of the game. Rather than running under an emulator, the real engine runs natively on Apple devices.

Writing about the port on GitHub, Reshi stressed that the work was a collaboration between a human and AI, not a case of just telling the AI to 'figure it out.' Claude handled the code and debugging, while a human did the playtesting. Problems such as 'the minimap is black' or 'there's a chirping sound' were described in words, and the model fixed them. In Reshi's words, "Neither half ships this alone: one of us can't write C++, and the other can't hear the chirping."

Could this work for other games? Nobody knows yet. Reshi himself is skeptical about Red Alert 2, since EA appears to have lost the source code. Even where source code survives, companies are unlikely to willingly allow a port that could hurt sales of a remaster or remake. There's also the lingering concern that an AI model could use the information it's given for training.

The cost wasn't trivial either. Reshi said he burned through his entire Claude Max subscription in two days. By his estimate, tokens alone cost between $100 and $200. He seems to believe Fable 5 is the only model that could pull this off, noting that Opus 4.8 couldn't manage it even with Ultra Code attached. There was no mention of whether he tried it on Google's own vibe coding platform.
So with a few hundred dollars, the game's source code, and an earlier port to reference, you can get the game running on an iPad in a single weekend. Simple, really.

Two Minute Papers covered the paper under the title 'They Said This Will Never Run In Real Time.' The paper itself is titled 'JGS2: Near Second-order Converging Jacobi/Gauss-Seidel for GPU Elastodynamics.' It presents a method for running elastic-body simulations of soft objects being pressed and bouncing back, in real time on a GPU.

In parallel simulation, convergence and parallelism routinely clash: boosting parallelism lightens local computation and weakens coupling, which slows overall convergence. Researchers led by Lei Lan looked into the 'overshoot' phenomenon, where a local solver reduces only its own energy while ignoring the global context and ends up ruining overall convergence, and reformulated the second-order optimal solution that suppresses it into a form that can be precomputed.

The results are striking. The method runs as parallel as the Jacobi method while converging nearly as well as Newton's method. It showed second-order convergence on both stiff and soft materials, converging 50 to 100 times better than existing state-of-the-art GPU methods. A domain once considered absolutely off-limits for real time has moved within reach of games and interactive simulation.
This is the MetaHuman 2026 sizzle reel unveiled at Unreal Fest Chicago. It brings together digital character work created with MetaHuman by teams around the world.

Epic explains that as the MetaHuman framework grows more powerful, examples showing just how far the technology can be pushed keep pouring in. The projects featured in the video span every industry, from games to film and TV, animation, and broadcast and live events.
Anyone who wants to try creating a realistic digital human can get started at metahuman.com.

This is a demo video Unity posted on its official channel. Unity AI automatically tags assets made with generative tools. Before release, you can scan the project for wherever generated assets are mixed in and swap out anything that seems off on the spot.
The video's description is short: generated assets get auto-tagged, making pre-release auditing and swapping easy. The Unity AI beta is free to try right now.
It's a short demo, but the target is clear. Figuring out which assets have gone through AI hands, project by project, comes first, and tagging is the starting point for that.

blocks.cap: Caveman (Image: Kotaku)

blocks.x: Costs are spiking across the AI world. Consumer devices, PC parts and games are all dealing with hardware shortages, and AI companies aren't doing much better. In recent weeks, several well-known AI companies have switched their subscriptions from flat-rate to usage-based pricing — a sign that the cost of keeping services running has become hard to bear, and even the big companies that embraced AI are getting more cautious. In the middle of it, some companies believe they've found a new fix: make AI talk like Tarzan.

According to 404 Media, a plugin is making the rounds among companies trying to cut token usage. Employees at several companies, including OpenAI, use 'Caveman,' a tool that tells models like Claude to talk not like SNL's Master Thespian, but like SNL's caveman lawyer.

"I made Caveman back in early April because I was using Claude Code heavily and noticed a lot of my token spend was going to unnecessary prose." That's what Julius Brussee, who built Caveman, told 404. The filler he singled out is "pleasantries, hedging, transitions, and chatty language that does not really matter."

Turn the plugin on, and responses that deliberately try to sound friendly and keep the conversation going shrink down to curt barks and growls. Instead of a gentle suggestion, you get a marching order. Brussee says lowering the AI's IQ cut token usage by about 65%.

Most things involving AI tend to feel like metaphors running wild, but this one is hard not to laugh at. For years, chatbots' human-level intelligence was the pitch, and now, faced with a cost calculation, it's basically a forced lobotomy. The AI industry and the race for funding have leaned heavily on pop culture's understanding of machine learning, going to absurd lengths to anthropomorphize language models. Once profit actually started to matter, the ground shifted fast. The cost of keeping AI services running is hard to bear, and no big company is naturally turning a profit yet. Earlier this year, OpenAI shut down its video generator Sora, which was burning $1 million a day, and that also tangled up its lucrative deal with Disney.

blocks.cap: Image: FC Tech Labs

blocks.x: A new action RPG on Steam sparked a debate among other developers. It started when its creator said generative AI was essential to speed up development, while also saying that more revenue could let them reduce that reliance.

Game developer and animator Aura Triolo (Bluesky: Aura/Moom) flagged the Steam AI disclosure text for Bahast, a new title billed as a dark fantasy idle ARPG. Triolo shared only the text, but others soon tracked down the game.

The issue remains a flashpoint in the debate over generative AI in games and development. When GamesRadar+ asked more than 30 developers, it heard a range of objections to generative AI as a tool, despite claims that it improves efficiency. A follow-up report focused more on indie developers' views is planned, and they were negative on the technology too.
Industry figures like Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney believe AI-integrated development will become essential going forward.
Several developers pushed back hard against Bahast's explanation. Triolo wrote, "'Give me money and I might use less AI' is the most desperate appeal I've ever seen."

David Lindsay Pittman of Minor Key Games, who made Eldritch, shot back, "'I'm just a small solo developer' doesn't work on solo and small developers like us, who've been making things without a picture-stealing scam machine."

Alexandre Strukov of Studio Alblune, maker of Squikross, said, "Learn to scale instead of whining." Solo developer Mtgames added, "I'm literally unemployed and I still make all my assets by hand. Why? Because it's fun."

Ryan Nurse, a solo developer at Altrix Studios, said, "Apart from Steam's distribution fee and the $5 I spent on TIC-80 Pro back in 2019, I haven't spent a single cent developing either Prism Indigo or Prism Warriors," adding, "'I have no money' is a nonsense excuse for using generative AI in games."

In a recent survey, not many Steam users took strong issue with AI in games. However, the people behind the survey warned that using AI still hurts sales, and said the questions and sample didn't quite match the broader user base.

blocks.cap: Image: Valve

blocks.x: It seems strange that while the whole world—or at least the gaming community—appears to speak with one voice against the spread of AI in games, game companies keep embracing the technology for efficiency, in many cases pushing out human jobs. A recent survey might help explain some of that gap.

In a recent survey from the GameDiscoverCo newsletter that polled 3,800 Steam users, a sizable share said they're largely fine with AI being used in games. Among respondents, 23.4% said "I have no problem with it at all," and 19.6% said "it's just fine."

Valve requires every developer to disclose on Steam whether and how much AI was used in a game. That means users, whatever their stance, can check the information before buying. There's something here for developers and publishers pushing AI to take note of: tolerance may be surprisingly high, but people are watching.

In another survey question, 44.4% of respondents said they "check carefully" whether a Steam game was made with AI assistance, 44.7% said they "skim it but don't care much," and 10.9% said they "don't read it at all." That means nearly 90% of Steam users generally check the AI disclosure before buying.

It's worth noting that respondents to these surveys don't represent the broader Steam user base. In GameDiscoverCo's words, they're "more engaged than average." Even so, it's useful for gauging how a certain segment of Steam users currently feels about AI in game development.

blocks.cap: Image: Sega

blocks.x: Even the Sega Dreamcast couldn't dodge AI. GamesRadar+ hardware editor Phil Hayton stopped scrolling mid-thumb. There, warped retro consoles and controllers, plus a VMU, carried smudged lettering and odd button symbols.

The keyring in question is an Anime Expo commemorative Dreamcast keychain sold on the Sega Shop. Shaped like the console body, controller, and even a VMU bearing a Chao sprite from Sonic Adventure, the item itself is pretty cute. If AI hadn't mangled the details, it would have been a covetable item for Sega collectors.

At a glance, nothing looks off. Only when you zoom in on the Sega logo does it become clear that it's not real lettering but scrawl-like lines, and the B on the controller button looks more like a messy circle.

blocks.cap: Image: Sega

blocks.x: Browsing the store, most of the Anime Expo lineup and regular merchandise used untouched images. Another offender is the Crazy Taxi air freshener set. Danny8bit flagged this earlier on X, and SEGAbits fed the actual artwork into a generative AI tool and reproduced the same kind of image. As laid out in a Time Extension report last month, that leaves room to hope the artwork itself wasn't made by AI.

It appears AI was used to place real product photos onto a particular background, and in the process mangled details that the AI couldn't properly reconstruct. Hayton wrote that he suspects these images are 'placeholders,' but added that it would be alarming if the AI details showed up unchanged on the actual products. He noted that Crazy Taxi: World Tour has already been criticized for using generative AI, and said he hopes a brand he cares about doesn't tumble into the pit of slop.

At the State of Unreal session at Unreal Fest Chicago 2026, Epic unveiled a workflow that uses image and video generation models alongside Unreal Engine tools. The goal is to let artists work with generated results with clearer intent and control.

It demonstrates matching generated results to the UE viewport's camera framing, creating variations that resemble scene elements already placed, and even restyling an entire scene to fit a project's requirements.
The feature is marked 'coming soon,' so it hasn't launched yet. The rest of the 5.8 updates are detailed on Epic's blog.

This is a Shorts video Unity posted on its official channel. The whole message in the description is that Unity AI cuts down the time spent on scene setup, so use that saved time to refine your ideas instead.

When AI assists with scene assembly inside the editor, repetitive work like initial placement gets lighter. It pairs with the automatic generative-asset tagging covered on the 7th, and the Unity AI beta is free to try right now.

Laura Miele, president overseeing corporate development at Electronic Arts, spoke about AI's role in game development. As developers hand off tedious tasks to AI tools, it frees up capacity for creative work — and that, she said, has led to a "real rise in creativity" inside EA.
Asked in an interview with The Game Business whether AI technology could speed up game development, Miele replied, "Perhaps in some parts they will."
She said removing "friction" from developers' work has long been something she wanted, and that adopting AI is already helping with that.

"I always have kind of wanted to be a hero to them and help them create career-defining experiences. And I think that AI—what I've seen—how AI has enabled removing friction from our pipelines and our tools and our workflows, has been pretty exciting. It's removed some tedium out of their jobs."

She didn't cite specific examples, but Miele said that using AI has sped up prototyping, and that she's also seen "faster creativity" — meaning less time between having an idea and seeing it realized. "So we're seeing it. I think there is a real rise of creativity that comes from removing some of the tedious tasks out of development."

The logic of offloading chores to AI so people can focus on creative work is a familiar talking point among industry executives. Witcher 3 director Konrad Tomaszkiewicz has said generative AI was essential to early development of the new game 'The Blood of Dawnwalker,' Take-Two chief Strauss Zelnick is likewise optimistic about using AI in non-creative areas, and Jeff Kaplan, known for Overwatch, has said AI has a place in certain parts of game production.

One thing worth noting: most of these comments come from executives and leaders, not from the people actually doing the hands-on work. A GDC survey that gauges sentiment on the ground found more developers than ever consider generative AI harmful to the game industry.

The Godot Foundation has announced it will revise the contribution policy for Godot, its free and open-source engine. Code contributions made with generative AI — that is, pull requests (PRs) — will no longer be accepted in almost all cases.

In a blog post published yesterday, the foundation noted that contributions submitted directly by AI agents, or by people submitting AI-generated code, have increased sharply in recent times. Of the maintainers who screen PRs, it wrote, "AI contributions have the added pain of being demoralizing."
The revision comes as studios keep pushing generative AI, even as developers themselves have held a predominantly negative view for years that the technology is eating away at the industry.

The foundation's stated principle is a single one: every contribution must be made by "someone who can take responsibility for their code" and who has the ability and willingness to fix it when needed. "AI cannot take responsibility, and we can't trust heavy users of AI to understand their code enough to fix it."

Going forward, the contribution policy will prohibit the use of autonomous AI agents, so-called vibe coding, generating substantial amounts of code with AI, and inserting AI-written text into communication between people.

There are exceptions. All code must be written by a human, but AI can be used for miscellaneous tasks like code completion, regular expressions, or find-and-replace. Anyone who used AI in any form must disclose that fact in the PR discussion.

The reasoning behind the communication rule is simple. Maintainers are volunteers who spend their own time reviewing issues, PRs, and proposals, and they don't want to talk to a machine. The foundation called this "a basic principle of respect." Machine translation is still allowed, however, as long as a human wrote the original text.

This announcement comes just weeks after Godot said it tolerates "some AI assistance" while rejecting the label of a "vibe coding engine." Back in February, veteran developer Remi Verschelde had also voiced frustration over the "AI slop" PRs flooding the engine.
The foundation closed with this: "The AI tools that exist today change every day. We will continue to maintain a conservative policy, but we will reevaluate if circumstances change."

Right after Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney criticized Valve over its mandatory AI-generated content disclosure, a browser plugin appeared that does the opposite — making that disclosure far more prominent and hiding AI games from search results. It's not something Sweeney will welcome.

A developer who goes by seeeeew, a self-described Linux gamer and coder, published the 'AI warning for Steam' plugin on Bluesky earlier this month — just before Sweeney said Steam's disclosure makes a game's chances of success "much, much, much harder."

The plugin is distributed for Firefox and Chrome, and is also up on GitHub. There are reports of a workaround that runs inside the Steam client itself, but this reporter wasn't able to verify that directly.

GamesRadar+ tested the Chrome version and confirmed it works as described. Opening the Steam store page of a game with an AI content disclosure makes that disclosure pop up right from the first screen, impossible to miss.

In search results, games that used AI are blurred out by default, with a label reading "AI Generated Content Disclosure found" overlaid on top. For anyone who treats the use of generative AI as a dealbreaker, it saves the trouble of checking games one by one.

The plugin got widespread attention during the recent Steam Next Fest, where demos of upcoming releases poured in. As Palworld lead John Buckley lamented, more and more Next Fest entries are using AI-generated images or assets.

Sweeney has repeatedly demanded that Steam drop the AI disclosure that doesn't exist on the Epic Games Store. He recently claimed the disclosure slaps a "Scarlet Letter" on games that use AI and draws in a "hate community trying to kill games." His argument is that developers must choose between giving up a tool that meaningfully boosts productivity and losing out to competitors, or accepting the stigma.
Yet in a GamesRadar+ feature that interviewed roughly 30 developers around the world, voices saying they don't want to use generative AI, for various reasons, came up again and again.

blocks.cap: Image: PC Gamer

blocks.x: The real headache with vibe coding isn't the output itself, but how shaky it is to build anything more on top of that codebase. AI agents are good at producing preferred outputs but can't 'think' through the next step, so AI code ends up full of duplication and inefficiency. That's where so-called 'AI slop' comes from.

According to Tom's Hardware, the team is called Slopfix. It strips out a set amount of unnecessary AI code and gets a cut of a $10,000 fee depending on how close it gets to the target. The example on its site is cutting 100,000 lines down to 35,000. Delete 65,000 lines and you get $10,000; cut only 32,500 and you get $5,000.

It's a common problem these days too. A few months ago, a popular PS3 emulator team asked users to stop "submitting AI slop code," and the open-source game engine Godot got buried in AI slop code earlier this year. Last month Godot decided to stop accepting AI-generated code contributions altogether, citing the difficulty of being able to "trust heavy users of AI to understand their code enough to fix it."

Cleaning up AI code doesn't solve the underlying problem of users not understanding their own output. It does, though, make it easier for AI agents to build more on top of it. Whether people will actually pay tens of thousands of dollars to have someone else clean up a codebase with the same tools is an open question. I wrote that I'm skeptical the Slopfix site was even made by a human hand to begin with, and its copy doesn't inspire much confidence either.

Still, one question lingers. If you pay an AI agent to fix the mistakes left by another AI's code, who's checking that the agent is actually doing the job right? And if three Slopfix engineers are combing through the code by hand, what was the point of using a coding bot in the first place?

This is a video Unity posted to its official channel. It shows Unity AI (beta) setting up and debugging animation state machines, behavior trees, and transitions from prompts alone. The point is to free up time from repetitive work so you can spend it polishing game feel instead.
Following the generative asset tagging and scene setup demos covered on the 7th and 8th, this shows another side of the Unity AI workflow. The Unity AI beta is free to try right now.

Amazon's AI slop book problem is likely still in its early stages. The company recently invested $50 billion in OpenAI and keeps pushing its poorly regarded in-house AI assistant Rufus everywhere. There's little sign the company will hold back the flood of slop books. One case that captures the absurdity perfectly: 'AI hallucination guides' for games that aren't even finished or released.

The Substack blog Rick's Game Backlog documented the phenomenon well. While searching Amazon to check game release dates, the writer found pricey guidebook listings for Alien: Isolation 2 (release date unannounced), Control: Resonant (September 24), and Gears of War: E-Day (October 6). All of them are available to buy right now.

The covers are all AI-generated, and the descriptions were written by AI too. In case any doubt remained, Rick's Game Backlog pointed to one passage. The description for a book with the sprawling title 'Gear of War E-Day Game Guide…' (not even 'Gears') opens like this: "Here is a high-converting Amazon-style book description crafted to sell your book while keeping it emotionally engaging, persuasive, and read-focused." You couldn't ask for a better opening line.

blocks.cap: A listing for an AI-generated guide on Amazon (Amazon / Kotaku)

blocks.x: Thankfully, Rick ordered a few of these books himself to show what's inside. The table of contents is printed as hyperlinks with no page numbers, and the book is laid out like a novel with not a single image, not even pretending to be a guide. After roughly 60 pages of AI-written world-building based on Wikipedia, chapters follow that 'walk through' features no game would ever have, like 'survival mechanics' or 'psychological warfare.' The Alien: Isolation 2 book even has an entire chapter covering system requirements that haven't been announced yet. Rick's Game Backlog reported the books to Amazon customer service and got them taken down, only for them to reappear immediately.

Legitimate guides do come out before release. Their authors get early access to unfinished builds and carefully document the content. This is a pile of nonsense plagiarized from online information. It's also a clever scam that piggybacks on Amazon's habit of recommending related products to people who've preordered. At more than $20, it's not cheap enough to slip by unnoticed either. The covers look plausible enough that a parent picking out a gift for a kid, or a gamer, could easily be fooled without suspecting a thing.

The same kind of AI slop guides are attached to already-released games too. There's a P book credited to 'author' George D. Brogan, who also wrote the Alien: Isolation 2 book, and the prolific guide-bot Donald C. Campbell has posted guides for The Adventures of Elliot and Mina the Hollower, and Star Fox. The Kotaku writer's favorite detail is that most of these books' descriptions contain some variation of "Step into the world of…"

An Amazon spokesperson told Kotaku, "We have content guidelines governing which books can be listed for sale and promptly investigate any book when a concern is raised," adding that books violating the guidelines get removed. After the article was first published, some of the offending books were taken down, only for identical copies to fill the same spot immediately.

blocks.cap: Magic: The Gathering 'Corrupt Court Official' art by Drew Baker (Wizards of the Coast)

blocks.x: Hasbro rarely gets a moment to catch its breath. PC Gamer's writer doesn't think it deserves one. Reports have emerged that the giant company behind Dungeons & Dragons and Magic: The Gathering is now pushing contracts that hand children's voice rights over to AI.

The basis is an open letter from the Agents of Young Performers Association, a group representing agents for child and teen actors, and Deadline's report connecting that letter to Peppa Pig. The letter reads: "A major studio who owns the IP for an international children's franchise producing a long running animated television series has offered contracts to child voice actors insisting that they agree to the use of AI thus allowing them to use the child's voice in all commercial assets within their franchise."

The letter continues: "The refusal to remove this clause with an attitude of 'take it or leave it' has led us [to] write this letter to make it clear that this will not be accepted and to bring this matter to the attention of the wider industry." Confirmed signatures have already passed 1,000.

Hasbro's track record over the past decade has been dismal. It sent Pinkerton detectives after fans who got hold of MTG cards early, laid off 1,100 people including key figures behind the deal that produced Baldur's Gate 3, and waged aggressive anti-union campaigns. Its CEO is enamored with AI. The company also lost Sigil, its virtual tabletop, and even canceled a game from the director of Jedi: Fallen Order.

If the open letter's accusations are true, it's a step too far even for a company whose reputation is already in the gutter. Rather than a specific response, Hasbro gave Deadline only this statement: "The protection of child performers is core to who Hasbro is, it's part of our DNA. As industry standards around AI continue to evolve, we are committed to engaging with this issue in a responsible and transparent manner."

PC Gamer's writer called the very idea of a contract letting AI use a child's voice chilling. In the end, it comes down to consent. An adult actor handing over similar rights is unpleasant enough, but that's the adult's own choice. There is no version of 'responsible and transparent' that applies to drawing a child, who needs a parent to understand and consent on their behalf, into a voice AI cloning contract.

It's not a good sign for Hasbro's games either. Voice actors have been wrestling with AI issues ever since the technology appeared, and it took a long strike to win fair contracts. That strike was something adults, capable of organizing and speaking up for themselves, could do. Children can't.

blocks.cap: Doki Doki Literature Club (Image: Serenity Forge)

blocks.x: Japanese IT media outlet ITmedia News first flagged this. The paper 'AI Fiction in the Wild,' presented at Purdue University's MFS Cultural AI Conference, analyzed 500,000 anonymized English ChatGPT conversations collected through WildChat, and one bizarre case stood out.

The study's purpose boiled down to examining the enormous number of AI prompts that amount to 'write me some fan fiction.' The sheer volume is staggering. The researchers wrote, "More than a third of the conversations contained some form of fiction generation." That figure covers original fiction and scripts, role-play, worldbuilding, fan fiction and erotica.

The study splits AI fiction users into two types: "Story cyclers ask for iterations of the same story for a period of time, then switch to another story or topic. Infinite story demanders request the same story, or a very similar one, over and over again for long stretches of time."

Among those infinite demanders, the single most prolific user's interest was oddly specific. Over several months, this person generated thousands of variations on a story about one of the girls from the visual novel Doki Doki Literature Club, mostly Natsuki, giving birth to a child. The child is usually a daughter named Sakura. The researchers even added a helpful footnote: "Sakura may be a reference to a character from the Naruto manga and anime series."

That power user wasn't alone either. "Two percent of users within the fiction subset are responsible for more than 80% of the conversations." A user fixated on pregnancy fiction skewed that figure upward, but the worlds most requested for fan fiction, in order, were Doki Doki Literature Club, League of Legends, Freedom Planet, and Naruto.

WildChat, the source of the data, is a free ChatGPT interface hosted on Hugging Face. It could be used on the condition that conversations would be anonymized and released for academic research, and the first public release alone, collected from April 2023 to May 2024, contained more than 500,000 English-language conversations.

What's interesting is that this AI fan fiction data looks nothing like what gets posted on AO3. Over the same period, stories based on Harry Potter, My Hero Academia, and Supernatural were far more common on AO3. In the human-written fan fiction world, writers encourage one another, and readers follow writers into other fandoms to find something new to love. It's a communal activity. PC Gamer noted that generating fiction with AI is, by comparison, a far more isolated act.

Recompiling classic games is becoming increasingly popular in PC gaming. The in-development 'Donkey Kong 64: Recompiled' project brings the 1999 N64 platformer classic to PC without relying on AI-assisted development.

YouTuber 2dos revealed a short teaser for the fan-made port on June 28. Built with Wiseguy's N64 recomp tool, the project converts the original code for the PC environment. Plans include widescreen support, higher frame rates, 4K resolution options, minigames tuned for low latency, and mod support.

As with other recompilation projects, the port does not include N64-version assets, so players must own the original game. That condition has let the related tools avoid takedown requests from Nintendo.

The 'DK64: Recompiled' development team previously made the popular 'Donkey Kong 64 Randomizer' mod. They draw a clear line between their work and so-called 'vibe coding,' in which code is generated and patched using AI.
Developer theballaam96 explained: "There's a competitor pushing through with vibe coding, and they're doing it very poorly."
The team stressed its experience, saying it has "people who have worked on DK64's code backend for over a decade" and "does not rely on vibe coding."
The PC Gaming Wiki recently removed such AI-assisted projects from its recompilation list, citing quality and stability issues. 'DK64: Recompiled' is now the only one listed in the official registry.

Dragon Age co-creator David Gaider sharply criticized the use of generative AI in game development. The former BioWare writer told GamesRadar that the technology is "terrible at repetitive tasks" and said flatly that generative AI output "has no soul."

Gaider served as lead writer on Dragon Age: Origins, Dragon Age 2, and Dragon Age: Inquisition. He pointed out that generative AI is often trained on data without creators' consent, raising both ethical and legal problems.

He said "generative AI is often trained regardless of whether the creator or owner consented to having their data pillaged," adding that this exposes projects to legal risk. He added that the argument "AI doesn't work properly unless we're allowed to steal what we need!" has no basis.

On AI-generated output, he asked, "Does it make the work more efficient? Does it make the output better?" Drawing on his narrative design experience, he said "fixing low-quality output took more time than just throwing it out and making it again."

People expect AI to handle the grunt work while humans focus on what matters, but Gaider said the reality he saw was the opposite — a setup where "AI does the important work, and the worker is there to 'clean up' after it."
He also warned against eliminating entry-level work: "If you eliminate all entry-level work, how are you going to train the next generation of developers?"
His conclusion was clear: until proper regulation and legally obtained training data are in place, "right now, it is a malignant plague, and it should be treated as one."
miHoYo, the developer of Genshin Impact, released not a traditional game but an AI companion app called BSide: Olivia Lin on Steam. The app is currently in early access and can be enjoyed for free.

The app's central character is Lin Li (Olivia Lin), a university student living in Shanghai. She majors in piano and minors in psychology, enjoys LP records, classic films, and rainy weather, and quietly explores the relationship between music and memory on her own.

There are four core features: listening to Olivia's piano performances; MIDI-to-MV, which turns an uploaded MIDI file into a music video; letters exchanged via AI; and a live wallpaper that puts her on the desktop. As an example of the MIDI feature, she was shown playing the melody of singer-songwriter Sheena Ringo's 'Marunouchi Sadistic.'
Users listen to her performances, exchange letters generated by AI text, and keep her nearby as a desktop widget to interact with.

miHoYo quietly launched BSide: Olivia Lin on Chinese Steam on June 22, 2026. The early access version is completely free. The interface, voice, and subtitles currently support only Simplified Chinese, and no schedule for English support or an overseas release has been announced.

On June 23, Sega announced a new Sonic the Hedgehog augmented reality game (ARG) called 'Chaos Hunt.' It asked players to recover Chaos Emeralds scattered across the United States to activate 'Club Chaos' this fall. But a backlash followed once participants learned they had to hand over personal information for AI training.

To take part in the game, players must submit their name, date of birth, zip code, and phone number. They must agree to Community's terms of service and privacy policy, and to "receive recurring messages related to Chaos Hunt (which may be marketing or automated) at the above number, from Sega or from Community on Sega's behalf."

Fans who read the fine print found an AI-related clause. The terms state that "your user data may be used to train and improve our proprietary AI models in order to improve the functionality, accuracy, and security of our services." They also permit data sharing with third-party vendors and let Sega retain the information even after the ARG ends.

The backlash was fast and fierce. One user wrote "fuck off Sega," while another wrote, "I thought Sonic was supposed to be against this kind of AI training, but okay, I guess." The original announcement got slapped with a community note, and the ratio on social media turned heavily against it.

Sega executives have signaled that adopting AI is inevitable. At a CEDEC 2025 presentation, technical directors Daishi Yokoshima and Atsuki Yagi said, "We are entering an era where we cannot avoid using AI." They said they are examining AI for "code generation, image generation, and motion generation" in internal tests, and mentioned the possibility of expanding into "automatic generation of story and dialogue."
The ARG appears to involve scanning QR codes at various locations, but since it has not fully begun, its overall scale and what Sonic-related announcement it will lead to remain unclear.

Sony filed a new annual report with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). As Stephen Totilo of Game File pointed out, the revised business outlook suggests Sony is now bracing for the possibility of falling revenue in the current market. It also removed language about bringing its first-party titles to PC.

Last year's report stated that PlayStation "aims for sustainable and profitable business growth." In this edition, that line was changed to "aims for sustainable business growth." Totilo saw the dropped word 'profitable' as a sign that soaring component prices are starting to weigh more heavily on PlayStation's earnings as well.

The report describes hardware this way: "In the hardware segment, Sony expects to be affected by rising memory semiconductor prices and supply shortages, but plans to manage the impact on profitability by flexibly adjusting unit sales volumes, promotions, and other factors."
In the meantime, Sony is looking to grow service-based revenue such as PlayStation Plus, a move that reads as an effort to offset thinner margins on hardware.

The direction of platform expansion has also shifted. Last year's report included a line saying Sony "plans to continue distributing first-party titles across multiple platforms, including PC." That passage has disappeared entirely from this year's report, which lines up with recent rumors that Sony hasn't gotten the profit and growth from the PC market that it had expected.

Recently, PlayStation CEO Hideaki Nishino effectively confirmed that single-player-focused first-party games will no longer come to PC. Release plans will depend on "the characteristics of each title," and live-service games with online elements will still be considered for PC releases to reach a wider audience. Single-player first-party games, on the other hand, will keep staying on PlayStation hardware. Nishino said, "Regardless of platform, we'll decide based on the principle of delivering the best gaming experience that maximizes each title's unique characteristics."

The AI-related passage also stands out. Sony said it will make broader use of AI-based tools in game development. The report states, "Sony is leveraging AI to draw out studio creativity and further enhance the PlayStation experience."

The report elaborates: "In our studio business, AI-based tools raise productivity, letting development teams reinvest the time they save into building richer worlds and play experiences. In our platform business, AI handles transactions more efficiently and personalizes content recommendations for individual users on the PlayStation Store. We also aim to continue investing in AI and machine learning to raise visual fidelity and deliver higher-quality play experiences."
Cross-media expansion continues as well. Sony plans to make films and TV series based on PlayStation game IP, aiming to broaden the reach and monetization of its intellectual property.

In recent years, documentaries that calmly dissect how computers actually work have multiplied. Dylan Reibling's 'The End of the Internet' points out that behind the elegant phrase 'cloud computing' lies a bundle of cables exposed to government valves and hungry sharks alike, while Amanda Kramer's 'So Unreal' traces how fantasies like The Matrix, Terminator, and Tron have shaped the public's understanding of cyberspace. It feels more relevant than ever now, when AI sales pitches feel like the final boss of the age of scams.

Adrian de Winter, a York University researcher and programmer, tried to show how easily we anthropomorphize technology through a somewhat Swiftian satirical paper. True to its title, 'If LLMs Have Human-Like Attributes, Then So Does Age of Empires II,' he used the scenario editor of the legendary RTS to recreate basic LLM functions with goats, grass, and bridges. He said he himself was surprised to find that, of the more than 300 papers he reviewed over the past two years, 57% started from the premise that AI has something resembling consciousness.

De Winter told 404 Media, "I pointed out that if goats could show emergent capabilities, that's great," and "these properties need to be preserved if we remove the chat panel. After all, it's not like your neurons know they are part of a brain." He added that research has long shown users easily grow attached when they sense warmth or personality in an LLM, noting that people don't bond with toasters but do bond with characters in movies.

In the paper, he avoids the term 'artificial intelligence' altogether, choosing the more precise phrase 'language learning model.' The study's aim was to show that once you strip away the friendly surface, the technology reverts to an unfamiliar block of code we already know well.

Kotaku's Zack Kotzer uses the paper as a springboard to criticize industry rhetoric. The promise of computers that think like people underpins the AI investment boom, but mimicking human tasks doesn't produce thought, intent, or reasoning. In his words, AI's consciousness amounts to the thirst of a drinking toy bird.

De Winter's proposal is clear: "I propose that we need to stop assuming that LLMs behave like humans just because they were trained with natural language. We should perform experiments that allow us to see LLMs as how they are, not how we believe they should be."
David Szymanski, the indie dev veteran known for Dusk and Iron Lung, isn't opposed to AI as a technology overall. But he has no interest whatsoever in making games with generative AI.

In an interview with GamesRadar+, Szymanski raised points in the same vein as a feature piece on why so many developers are averse to generative AI. He said that discussing the technology requires addressing ethical concerns around plagiarism, environmental burden, and jobs first, and that alone is enough to put him off the technology in its current form.

Even if all those barriers were cleared, for Szymanski generative AI is still "a complicated machine for generating subpar stock photos, buggy code, and a big neon sign for your audience that says 'I don't give a fuck,' and I'm not really in the market for any of those."

He believes AI simply isn't suited to creative work from the outset. There may be areas where it could genuinely help, he said, but he still has too many concerns about the harm the technology is causing and could cause, and if it's used at all, it needs to be useful in a way that doesn't damage the important parts of the creative process.

As he sees it, the appeal of AI today lies in being fast and easy. Some jobs call for fast and easy, but others call for slow and hard. His view is that creativity reveals itself in the process of solving the problems that appear between an idea and the finished work. "Your creative voice is defined by your limitations and how you work around those limitations." Hand all those problems over to a copying algorithm, and there's nothing left to separate the finished work from the original the algorithm copied.

He said flatly that developers have no say in how the industry ends up treating generative AI. All they can decide is how they personally respond, and whether or not to go along with the trend. "In its current form I don't have any interest in generative AI as a development tool and I don't think my audience has any interest in me using it either."
80 Level got hands-on with Hi3D, an AI 3D creation tool. Entering a single sentence produced a fully assembled 3D character model ready to print immediately.
This is a hands-on report that looks at the text-to-3D-asset pipeline from a creator's perspective. It shows step by step how an idea becomes a physical figure you can hold in your hand.
For game and asset artists who want to quickly test character prototypes, it's a workflow they can put to use right away. The distance from imagination to a physical object has narrowed further.
Confusion spread around “Gunny,” the loadout helper in Modern Warfare 4. Developer Infinity Ward made clear that Gunny is not a conversational chatbot.

To borrow their phrasing, Gunny is closer to “Windows' Clippy, but for building loadouts.” It's just a rule-based guidance feature that helps with weapon combinations, a different thing from a generative language model.
That doesn't mean the game has no AI at all. Infinity Ward confirmed it does use AI, in areas outside of Gunny. It's a moment that reveals where an AAA studio draws the line on what it calls AI.

Roblox unveiled a mobile app called “Build.” Typing in a natural-language sentence produces a simple game that can be played right away. It's an attempt to lower the barrier to making something on the platform.

The company made clear that what this produces won't flood the homepage with cheap “slop.” It explained that this isn't meant to replace existing Studio production lines, but to serve as an entry point for newly arriving creators.
It stands out as a text-to-game case coming from a massive UGC platform. At the same time, it leaves open new questions about how discoverability and quality control will be handled.
An iOS developer built and released a mobile game called “Capybara Food Delivery.” All of its roughly 27,000 lines of code were written by Claude Code using “vibe coding.”
The game won a competition with a $25,000 prize. It stands as a tangible example of a game completed entirely with AI-written code, from start to finish.
It offers a sense of how far prompt-driven development has come, beyond simple autocomplete assistance.

Sony executives have defined AI, particularly the kind that generates “synthetic assets” for game development, as a foundational technology underpinning the company's strategy. They even called it “interesting.”
Executives see AI spanning production efficiency, player experience and content discovery alike. A major first-party publisher has openly embraced a generative asset pipeline.
It's a sign that AI is moving firmly into AAA production.

The co-op hide-and-seek game Meccha Chameleon has been sweeping Steam lately. Resembling Prop Hunt, it sold 7 million copies in under two weeks of launch. As soon as it became a hit, a copycat followed close behind—a game called Scribble Hunt showed up on Steam with screenshots that look nearly identical to Meccha Chameleon.

Made by an obscure studio called Scribble Bunny, this game copies the original down to its description. The pitch—paint a rabbit-person to blend into the background like a chameleon—and the 2-to-10-player online hide-and-seek format are both carried over as is. It also carries a notice that some of the store images and promotional art were made with generative AI.

It's a clear picture of how cheap AI content pipelines can copy a hit game within days and dump it onto the store. After the success of lemorion_1224, who made the original, it's become an environment where a knockoff with a slightly tweaked name and design can show up at any time.

Porting old console games to PC has lately become a stage for emotional clashes. The clearest example is DK64 Recompiled, revealed in late June. The randomizer community, which has spent years taking this game apart and reassembling it, decided to build its own official PC port in response to an AI-rushed port carrying the same name.

Behind this is a technique called static recompilation, which moves the original code wholesale into another system language, unlike emulation, which mimics hardware. Thanks to N64 Recomp, released two years ago, games like Banjo-Kazooie, Star Fox 64, and Mario Kart 64 have been ported to PC. Because it doesn't bundle the original assets and instead has users supply their own ROM, it stays legally clean.

The problem is the vibe-coded ports flooding out almost daily these days. One developer used Claude to churn out recompilation tools for the NES, Sega Genesis, PlayStation, and SNES, while another opened repositories spanning everything from the PS3 to the ZX Spectrum. Balam, a contributor to the DK64 randomizer, says recomps that lean heavily on AI aren't even promoted anymore on the main N64 recomp server.

2dos names technical debt as the biggest risk. If developers don't properly understand AI-written code, maintenance becomes "a nightmare," and they end up burning more tokens just chasing bugs. In the AI version of Donkey Kong 64, reportedly, RT64, the core module that renders N64 graphics, had been tampered with. That's why the Godot engine and projects on the GameCube/Wii and PS1 side have, one after another, drawn the line: "we don't use AI code."

Two Minute Papers covered Minecraft this time. In a mod called Terrain Diffusion, a diffusion model generates the game's terrain directly. Minecraft normally stamps out terrain using a hand-tuned noise function, a method prone to producing mountains and valleys with monotonously repeating textures.

Terrain Diffusion brings the same diffusion models used for image generation straight over to height maps. Starting from random noise, it refines the terrain step by step, shaping more varied and natural-looking mountain ranges that follow the distribution of real terrain it learned from. The video places it side by side with existing noise-generated terrain to show the difference.

The key point is that this isn't just a demo stuck in a paper. The creator (xandergos) has posted the mod on Modrinth and GitHub, so anyone can download it and drop it into their own Minecraft. For game designers and modders, it's a case of generative AI crossing over into a procedural content generation tool they can actually get their hands on.

NVIDIA unveiled a beta of the ACE Game Agent SDK and an Unreal Engine 5 plugin at Unreal Fest 2026. This video walks developers through building an AI NPC directly inside Unreal Engine 5.7 using those tools. The key is running speech recognition, a small language model, and speech synthesis all on the device to cut latency.

The ACE Game Agent SDK is a lightweight C/C++ agent framework that plugs directly into a game. It's open source, so it can be freely modified, and it's accelerated on NVIDIA RTX hardware tuned for small models. The API splits into three parts. The Agent API manages conversation history and drives multi-step reasoning. The Chat API directly controls inference and responses. The RAG API handles retrieval-augmented generation, tying answers to a knowledge base the developer specifies.

In Unreal Engine 5.7, MetaHuman NPCs run on-device. Riva Parakeet ASR handles real-time speech recognition, while Chatterbox TTS handles emotionally expressive voice synthesis. Audio2Face moves the face to match the speech.
Because none of it goes to the cloud, it all runs on-device for fast responses. This changes how studios build conversational characters in the first place.

NVIDIA also presented real-world examples. Krafton introduced an AI teammate named Ally in Battlegrounds, which listens to players by voice, reads the situation, and reacts in real time — all running on-device on GeForce RTX. Total War: Pharaoh's advisor searches more than 1,200 game data tables to answer strategy questions.

These days, barely a day goes by without news that some famous director has embraced AI as the future of creativity or joined forces with it. This time it's none other than the father of Star Wars, George Lucas — and the logic is more than a little bitter.

In an interview with A Rabbit's Foot, Lucas talked about his career and the Lucas Narrative Art Museum, opening in Los Angeles this fall. The museum showcases decades of handmade art and, as its website puts it, shines a light on “stories and the people who tell them.” In the interview, he also shared insights on filmmaking, his collaborations with people like Steven Spielberg, and remarks on the pitfalls of preview focus groups.

“If an audience doesn't like a certain character, that's interesting, and as a director I want to know why,” he says. “But studios misread that. They let the audience make the movie themselves. These days it's gone too far — it's all about what the fans think. That's not how you make a movie. You need to find someone who knows how to make a film, has a story to tell, and has passion for it, for it to become a movie.”

Yet having just championed human-centered creation, he immediately turns around and calls AI the “future,” comparing not using the new technology to clinging to outdated transportation in the age of the automobile.

“Artificial intelligence lets us make movies much more easily,” he says. “It's like sitting here saying, ‘I believe the horse carriage is the real thing. Cars break down, you have to put gas in them, they're full of problems. Soon they'll turn them into tanks and kill people with them. It's terrible.’ There's nothing you can do about it. That's progress, that's the future.”
When A Rabbit's Foot pressed further, Lucas acknowledged the risks of plagiarism machines but didn't back down, pointing instead to other benefits he says AI will bring in the future.

“If you want AI that can tell you whether something is fake or where it came from, AI can do that,” he says. “Humans can't. We're not smart enough for that. The key thing is that you're human, and you're accountable for what you say and do. If you break the law, you should be punished. Whatever you do, it tends to come out eventually. It's just like reality.”

In 'Star Wars Episode V: The Empire Strikes Back,' there's a scene where Luke Skywalker, training as a Jedi with Yoda, asks whether the dark side of the Force is stronger than the light. Yoda says it isn't, but answers that many fall to the dark side because it's “quicker, easier, more seductive.” It's a 46-year-old film, but it captures the logic Lucas is using right now rather well.

He champions the importance of human-made art, yet argues that a technology notorious for stealing from humans — and whose output is usually worse than handmade work — makes filmmaking “easier.” Holding both the belief that the human spirit is what makes great films and the belief that a technology which strips away that humanity is the future of film is a contradiction. Even if it's naive, even if it goes against the grain, I'll keep standing against it.

Mega Crit is deliberately putting “crappy” hand-drawn placeholder art into its new roguelike, Slay the Spire 2, instead of AI-generated images. Casey Yano, co-founder and lead on the game, says it's not just about avoiding the appearance of laziness — it's “important” that unfinished art openly looks unfinished.

In an interview with GameSpot, Yano explained Slay the Spire 2's approach to placeholder art. You can see plenty of it in the game's timeline sequences, looking almost like it was drawn in MS Paint. Yano said that's very much intentional.

Since the game is still in Early Access, he “wanted to make it clear that some elements are unfinished.” At the initial launch in March, the artists may have wanted to finish more art, but Yano said he “knew they'd be drawing a lot of garbage-looking art during Early Access,” and that the unfinished feel matters because otherwise “people will judge this game like it's a finished 1.0 game.”
He goes on: “If you use art that looks almost finished, people assume that's the final art. It needs to look rough. Looking rough matters.”

That doesn't mean the placeholder art has no job to do, though. Yano especially wants the art used in the timeline to serve as a kind of “frame.” Those drawings are key narrative beats, meant to properly convey the planned composition, detail, and color.

On AI-generated art, Yano was clear about where he stands: “If you've gone through the artistic process… you might not say you felt cheated, but you'd feel a kind of sadness, because you can't see the path someone took to build their skill and develop their own style.” He also noted that the game already has its own style, so there's no reason to use AI to imitate it.

Hand-drawn work has “a decision behind nearly every line, down to a single erased line or a single refining stroke,” he says. AI art, by contrast, has a distinct look that's “very dense, flashy, and pronounced,” which clashes with the rest of the art style and “just feels lazy.”

Yano isn't rejecting AI outright. For some programmers who use it in code review, he says AI is basically a “fancy spell-checker.” Generative AI, though, is a different matter, and the team keeps it at a distance. To him, art isn't something with a “definable end goal” — it's a form of “expression.”

Just the concept of AI-based “vibe coding” is enough to make us spit out our strawberry matcha latte, but Circana industry analyst Mat Piscatella thinks it's about to make Steam and other game storefronts even worse.

Nothing grows in our bleak world anymore — not physical PlayStation discs, not originality, not anything that isn't AI slop. As a prime example, 404 Media reported that thanks to AI vibe coding, developers can now effectively clone someone else's video game, sometimes in a matter of dozens of hours. Piscatella reacted to the news on Bluesky, writing: “Good games are going to be cloned and buried. Players will gravitate toward games and franchises they know and trust. It will be harder to stand out.”
Just in case, as Piscatella put it, this is a situation some experts would call “not good. Not good at all.”

AI knockoffs that rip off successful games — especially indie darlings with social buzz but no team of copyright lawyers — are already scattered across most major storefronts. Think the fake “Peak” on the PlayStation Store or the knockoff “REPO” on the Nintendo eShop. Browsing Steam is already overwhelming now, and it's chilling to imagine these storefronts getting filled with even more AI junk going forward.

Of vibe coding, Piscatella says it's “a strong counterargument to people who claim AI will help the game market by lowering development time and cost.” “Add that to the already enormous discoverability problem — the explosion in the number of games launching per day — plus demand that's matured… bad!”
Still, isn't there something someone could do? Shouldn't mega-corporations at least on the scale of Sony and Nintendo be doing better quality control?
“At this point, it doesn't look stoppable,” Piscatella says. “As for a solution… yeah, if I knew how to solve this, I'd be out there doing it right now and getting ready to buy an island.”
Well, what can you do. Just another day in paradise.
Earlier this year, we talked to dozens of game developers and heard the many reasons they don't want to use generative AI.
Solo developers use AI coding tools to churn out playable clones of indie games within days. Sometimes they list the clone before the original even ships.
It is a concrete shift upending how small studios reveal and protect their work in progress.
The hit game Meccha Chameleon is establishing itself as a human-made counterweight to the wave of AI-generated content and imitators flooding the storefronts.
It presents hand-crafted chaos as an edge that sets it apart from generative pipelines, a rebuttal told in the language of craft and design.

Dear Passengers is a co-op game where you and your friends fly a plane, look after passengers, and complete missions. You'll be wrestling with ragdoll physics, random events, and above all each other's clumsiness. Think of it as similar to Peak, just set on an airplane.

Wishlists piled up by the hundreds of thousands in a single day, and it spread like wildfire on social media. It was shaping up to be the next indie friend-slop to swallow a whole weekend, until a few people flagged some unflattering details.

One character nameplate in the trailer reads Epst. J. An explanation surfaced claiming it's short for the Dutch European Pilot Selection & Training, but with a J tacked on, it reads as a reference to Jeffrey Epstein. There's also a character named PDaddy.
